Q: Pandas get first negative number from the bottom A:

Here I am using Polars to solve this question. Useful for Polars Lovers !!!

import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "rice":    [100, -10,  50, -20, -5],
    "outcome": [1000, None, 2000, None, None],
})

df = df.lazy().with_row_index('idx')

lastOutcomeIdx = pl.col('idx').filter(pl.col('outcome').is_not_null()).max().fill_null(-1)


# phycially after the Boundary Wall( index > lastOutcomeIdx) 
m1 = pl.col('idx') > lastOutcomeIdx 
m2 = pl.col('rice') < 0
mask = m1 & m2 

firstNegetiveIdx = pl.when(mask).then(pl.col('idx')).otherwise(None).min()


aa = df.with_columns(firstNegetiveIdx.alias('firstNegetiveIdx'))

mask1 = pl.col('idx') == pl.col('firstNegetiveIdx')

res = aa.with_columns(
    pl.when(mask1)
      .then(pl.lit('XXXXX'))
      .otherwise(None)
      .alias("first negative from last")
).collect()

print(res)
'''
┌─────┬──────┬─────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ idx ┆ rice ┆ outcome ┆ firstNegetiveIdx ┆ first negative from last │
│ --- ┆ ---  ┆ ---     ┆ ---              ┆ ---                      │
│ u64 ┆ i64  ┆ i64     ┆ u64              ┆ str                      │
╞═════╪══════╪═════════╪══════════════════╪══════════════════════════╡
│ 0   ┆ 100  ┆ 1000    ┆ 3                ┆ null                     │
│ 1   ┆ -10  ┆ null    ┆ 3                ┆ null                     │
│ 2   ┆ 50   ┆ 2000    ┆ 3                ┆ null                     │
│ 3   ┆ -20  ┆ null    ┆ 3                ┆ XXXXX                    │
│ 4   ┆ -5   ┆ null    ┆ 3                ┆ null                     │
└─────┴──────┴─────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
'''

Q: Pygame platformer: player sticks to the side of stacked tiles during collision A:

I think the problem is that as you're looping through all the tiles, the first check is for "Vertical collisions". I think that's the thing that is setting the player.vel_y to 0, causing them to "stick".

To fix that, you need to check to see if the user is next to or under the tile. So compare the x "left" and x "right" of the player and the tile to see if you need to even check for the vertical collision.

You might want to even make a separate function that returns the tiles that the player is currently colliding with.

Also, it looks like there are some functions to help with collision detection: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html?highlight=collide

If you're looking to learn and work on manual collisions, this is an older, simple, but effective, game engine written for JavaScript. I remember their collision system being very straightforward (relatively): https://github.com/phoboslab/impact

That might give you more insight into what type of checks you need to do, in what order, and how to optimize them. Currently, with your main loop, the bigger the level, the slower your collision system is going to go.

Q: fgets doesn't return NULL when it reaches to the EOF A:

How can I detect if there are still new lines in a file without having trouble ending the program?

Keep calling fgets(inst, SIZE, fp) until it returns NULL due to an end-of-file.

it failed in ending itself.

Code failed to check the return value of fgets(). So code repeatedly processes the old data as nothing new was written to it.

Another contributing cause: See fgets() with buffer 1 below

OP's approach is flawed. Should fgets() not read anything due to end-of-file, the buffer is not changed.

fgets(inst, SIZE, fp);
while (*inst == ' ') { // Bad. `inst` may be uninitialized data or left-over data.

Before using inst, check the return value.

        if (fgets(inst, SIZE, fp) == NULL) {
          break;
        }
        while (*inst == ' ') {

fgets doesn't return NULL when it reaches to the EOF

IMO, an incorrect functioning fgets() for this pathologically corner case of using a size 1 buffer.

fgets() with a buffer size of 1 is tricky. In theory, it should return feof(stream) ? NULL : buffer as it is only big enough to not read any data and then append null character. Yet this functionality is not well specified nor well implemented. I would not be surprised to see fgets() here always return the same value (e.g. the buffer pointer).

static inline bool potentially_hasMoreLines(char* inst, FILE* fp) { return !feof(fp); } is closer to OP's goal, yet either approach is not predictive. Reading needs to reach the end first, before the end-of-file indicator is set.

It is not clear that the string is shorter as the null character is not re-written.

for (int i=0;*(inst+i) != '\0';i++) {
  *(inst+i) = *(inst+i+1);
}


---

Code likely has other issues too.

Q: PostGIS - Create Ellipse A:

Here's an alternative approach to solving your problem.

  1. Create the ST_GeoAstroide() function from the PostGeoSQL library, Link https://github.com/CM-FOGS/PostGeoSQL/blob/main/ST_GeoAstroide

  2. Convert the function's parameter values ​​from meters to degrees. For example, 110 meters is approximately 0.00098816 (semi-major axis), 100 meters is approximately 0.000898327 (semi-minor axis), and the compression ratio will be 0.00098816 ÷ 0.000898327 = 1.10000033395412.

If you want to compress the circle along the X axis, set the required values ​​in the function as shown in the code.

SELECT ST_SetSrid(ST_MakePolygon(ST_MakeLine(ST_GeoAstroide(geom, 0.00098816, i, 1, 1.10000033395412, 1, 1))),4326) geom FROM (SELECT ST_Point(8.54736328125, 46.37156925087649) geom) foo CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series (0,360) AS step(i);

If you want to compress the circle along the Y axis, set the required values ​​in the function as shown in the code.

SELECT ST_SetSrid(ST_MakePolygon(ST_MakeLine(ST_GeoAstroide(geom, 0.00098816, i, 1, 1, 1, 1.10000033395412))),4326) geom FROM (SELECT ST_Point(8.54736328125, 46.37156925087649) geom) foo CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series (0,360) AS step(i);

SELECT ST_Rotate(geom, -pi()/4, ST_Centroid(geom)) geom FROM ellipse;

Q: aiohttp: rate limiting parallel requests A:

Like Filip suggested, using a dedicated wrapper is definitely cleaner than hacking together your own Semaphores or decorators.

I built http-wizz to take this approach a step further. It reduces the boilerplate (no need to define custom callback functions) and solves the "queueing vs execution" problem by using a Token Bucket to throttle the actual network calls, not just the task creation.

Here is the 50 RPS solution:

# pip install http-wizz
from http_wizz import WizzClient

async def main():
    urls = ["https://api.example.com/resource/1", ...]

    # Strictly enforces 50 RPS.
    # Automatically pauses if the server sends a "Retry-After" header.
    async with WizzClient(requests_per_second=50) as client:
        results = await client.fetch_all(urls)

One powerful feature that might help if you are aggregating data from different sources is Domain Specific Limits. You can set a high global rate while throttling specific, slower APIs:

# 50 RPS global, but throttle 'fragile-api.com' to 2 RPS
client = WizzClient(
    requests_per_second=50, 
    domain_limits={"fragile-api.com": 2}
)

If you need full control (POST/PUT/Headers) like the TentacleSession example above, http-wizz also provides a drop-in RateLimitedSession that works exactly like aiohttp.ClientSession but with these safety rails built in.

Check out the package here: https://github.com/TomMcKenna1/http-wizz

Q: Is there a RegExp.escape function in JavaScript? A:
